title: Cascade synchrony spectrogram — personal run log
content:
Quick summary:
- Goal: understand recurring p99 spikes that correlate with a ~8–12s periodicity on the A100 pool during mixed short+medium seq workloads. Suspect request arrival synchrony (small cascade windows) + KV cache pressure.
- Approach: synthetic spectrogram-style visualization of request density vs latency over time + controlled traffic generator that can insert small synchronized windows.

Hypothesis:
- Short synchronized bursts (many requests aligned to a narrow time window) create transient KV cache churn and GPU context switches -> p99 spikes even when p50/p95 look fine.
- If true, breaking synchrony (jitter) or smoothing request starts should reduce p99 without harming throughput.

Experiment setup:
- Cluster: dedicated-A100-pool (4x A100:40GB). Single model shard per GPU (gpt-medium-16k-quant), KV cache enabled.
- Traffic generator: custom wrk2-like harness (local binary: ./gen-traffic) with options: poisson arrivals, fixed-window (synchrony), jittered-window.
- Sequence length mix: 20% short (64 tokens), 60% medium (512 tokens), 20% long (2048 tokens). Tokenization deterministic.
- Concurrency cap at gateway: 120 concurrent requests. Autoscaler disabled for test window.
- Observability: prom queries for request_rate, in_flight, model_kv_evictions, gpu_util, and custom hist:latency_ms. Collected into local CSV every 1s.

Key commands (run on bench node):
- synchronized window run:
  ./gen-traffic --mode fixed-window --window-width 200ms --qps 450 --duration 120s --dist mix20-60-20 > run_fixedwindow_2025-01-20.log
- jittered window run (gaussian jitter 120ms sd):
  ./gen-traffic --mode jittered-window --window-width 200ms --jitter-sd 120ms --qps 450 --duration 120s --dist mix20-60-20 > run_jitter_2025-01-20.log
- poisson baseline:
  ./gen-traffic --mode poisson --qps 450 --duration 120s --dist mix20-60-20 > run_poisson_2025-01-20.log

Prom queries used (examples):
- request rate (1s): sum(rate(redwood_requests_total[1s]))
- p99 latency (last 2m): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (le)) * 1000
- kv evictions: sum(rate(kv_cache_evictions_total[1s]))

Raw run observations (snippets):
- fixed-window run (first 60s): periodic p99 spikes every ~9s, amplitude 220–320ms. p50 steady ~18ms. gpu_util shows brief dips coincident with spikes. kv_evictions spike at same times (0 -> 50 evictions/sec).
- jittered-window: p99 reduced to 110–140ms peaks, less regular. kv_evictions lower and spread out.
- poisson: smoothest profile, p99 ~95–120ms, no regular periodicity.

Quantitative summary (aggregated over 2m after steady-start):
- fixed-window: p50=18ms, p95=54ms, p99=275ms, avg_throughput=432 qps, kv_evictions_peak=52/s
- jittered-window: p50=19ms, p95=48ms, p99=128ms, avg_throughput=428 qps, kv_evictions_peak=18/s
- poisson: p50=17ms, p95=46ms, p99=102ms, avg_throughput=435 qps, kv_evictions_peak=10/s

Spectrogram visualization notes (how I built it):
- Inputs: 1s-binned latency percentiles and request counts. Constructed 2D heatmap (time vs frequency band) where color intensity = p99 latency magnitude scaled; overlay request-rate as line.
- Fixed-window plot shows vertical bright stripes every ~9s aligning with request-rate peaks -> strong synchrony signal.

Initial conclusions / working takeaways:
1) Synchrony of arrivals (even narrow ~200ms windows) amplifies cache churn and leads to transient p99 spikes; throughput remains high but tail latency suffers.
2) Injecting small jitter (100–150ms) to request start times substantially reduces p99 with minimal throughput impact. This is a cheap mitigation for client SDKs or edge gateways.
3) GPU utilization dips during spikes — suggests KV cache misses cause extra compute and/or scheduling imbalance; investigate whether CPU-side scheduling/backpressure also contributes.

Short-term mitigations to try next:
- Client SDK: add jitter sampling of start times (configurable jitter-ms). A/B vs control in staging.
- Gateway smoothing: linear tokenized slow-start (ramp a requests over 100–300ms) rather than all-at-once.
- Increase KV cache partitioning heuristics to reduce eviction clumping (experiment with cache shard counts + TTL per tenant).

Longer-term / infra changes to test:
- Adaptive admission: when request_rate shows narrow spectral peaks, throttle briefly or route to warmened pool.
- Kernel/runtime: investigate prefetching KV for likely next tokens to reduce miss penalty.
- Scheduler improvements: reduce preemption/scheduling variance across GPUs during these windows.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Is the periodicity coming from client batchers (SDKs) hitting sync points (cron-like)? Need to correlate with ingress logs from customers.
- Is this effect model-size dependent? Repeat with smaller model shard (gpt-small) and larger (gpt-large) to compare eviction sensitivity.
- How do multi-tenant mixes behave when one tenant synchronizes while others are steady?

Notes / TODOs:
- [ ] Run same fixed-window test at 2x qps and 0.5x qps to see non-linear scaling of p99.
- [ ] Run with H100 fleet to check whether HW differences mitigate the scheduling dips.
- [ ] Ask infra to pull kube-scheduler logs for the exact spike times (2025-01-20 14:12:XX etc.).
- [ ] Post short writeup to #infra-ops and propose client-side jitter flag as an immediate mitigation.

Attachments / references (local):
- run_fixedwindow_2025-01-20.log (raw), run_jitter_2025-01-20.log, spectrogram_fixedwindow_2025-01-20.png
- local notebook: ~/bench/spectrogram_analysis.ipynb

Random heuristics I tried (notes):
- increased per-GPU cache size by 10% -> reduced peak evictions by ~12% but p99 remained ~200ms for fixed-window (so cache size alone not sufficient).
- added a token-prefetch hook (slow prototype) reduced spike amplitude in a single run, needs more runs.

If anyone picks this up: start by re-running the fixed-window vs jitter comparison on a fresh day (no other experiments), attach kube events and node-level dmesg around spike times. I'll mock a short PR for SDK jitter flag after we confirm with one more run.

-- Leah
